strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: existing evaluation protocols in visual brain decoding (such as two-way identification and low-level image metrics like SSIM/PixCorr) have become saturated, noisy, or decoupled from human perception.

Rigorous meta-evaluation supported by a newly collected human judgment dataset comprising 1,000 test image pairs evaluated by 22 annotators, showing that SEED correlates significantly better with human semantic judgments (Kendall's Tau = 0.621, Pearson = 0.817) than existing metrics.

Insightful error and case analysis, clearly illustrating why individual components (Object F1, Cap-Sim, EffNet) fail in isolation and how their combination provides complementary coverage over semantic content, scene context, and global representations.
Formalization of the 'semantic near-miss' phenomenon, providing valuable qualitative and quantitative insight into the systematic failure modes of state-of-the-art brain decoding systems.

The proposed pairwise hinge loss offers a plug-and-play auxiliary objective that consistently improves semantic alignment across multiple existing decoding frameworks (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain).
weaknesses: The human judgment data was gathered exclusively on reconstructions produced by a single model architecture (MindEye2). Validating metric correlations across diverse model families (e.g., GAN-based vs. diffusion-based, or non-CLIP conditioning) would strengthen claims regarding generalizability.
Object F1 is restricted to 82 pre-defined object categories (COCO + man/woman), which limits its ability to evaluate open-world visual stimuli that contain unlisted object classes.
The pairwise hinge loss incurs an O(N^3) memory/computational complexity due to the three-way tensor construction [N, N, N], which may constrain scaling to larger mini-batch sizes.

Performance gains provided by the pairwise hinge loss on the strongest baseline (MindEye2) are relatively marginal (SEED increases from 0.474 to 0.475 in Table 3), although gains are clearer on MindBridge and UniBrain.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely issue in visual brain decoding: existing evaluation schemes (especially two-way identification tasks) are largely saturated, pool-dependent, and often fail to penalize severe semantic misalignments.

Provides a well-grounded meta-evaluation supported by a dedicated human evaluation benchmark (1,000 test image pairs across 22 annotators), demonstrating that SEED aligns significantly better with human semantic judgments than prior metrics.

The proposed metric SEED effectively captures complementary aspects of image semantics: fine-grained object presence via threshold-averaged Object F1, natural language visual descriptions via Cap-Sim, and holistic feature representations via EffNet.

Offers valuable analytical insights into the visual decoding domain, notably through detailed failure case analyses of individual metrics and the systematic quantification of the 'semantic near-miss' phenomenon.

Proposes a general pairwise hinge loss ($L_{pair}$) that consistently improves embedding alignment and semantic reconstruction quality across multiple existing baselines (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain).
weaknesses: The human judgment dataset used for meta-evaluation is collected solely on reconstructions generated by a single model (MindEye2), leaving open the question of whether human alignment generalizes equally well across fundamentally different model families or failure distributions.

SEED relies on multiple large pretrained foundation models (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer, EfficientNet), making the metric computationally heavier than standard metrics and subject to the vocabulary restrictions (e.g., 82 classes in Object F1) and perceptual biases of these upstream models.

The performance gains provided by the proposed pairwise hinge loss on competitive models such as MindEye2 are modest (e.g., SEED increases from 0.474 to 0.475 in Table 3), and the $O(N^3)$ complexity of the triplet-like formulation may limit scaling to larger batch sizes.

Combining Object F1, Cap-Sim, and EffNet via a simple arithmetic mean is heuristic; the components have different score distributions and dynamic ranges, and alternative weighting or normalization strategies are not extensively explored.

strengths: Important problem addressed: The paper identifies critical shortcomings in existing visual brain decoding evaluation schemes—specifically the saturation and comparative flaws of 2-way identification metrics, as well as the poor correlation of metrics like SSIM/PixCorr with human semantic perception.

Well-structured human meta-evaluation study: The authors gathered 22 human ratings across 1,000 ground-truth/reconstruction pairs, providing empirical grounding to benchmark current metrics against human semantic judgment.

Insightful diagnostic analysis: The identification and quantification of the 'semantic near-miss phenomenon' (accounting for 17.5%–20.6% of salient object errors) provides valuable insights into the specific failure modes of current fMRI decoding models.

Clear presentation and thorough ablation: The paper clearly justifies why individual metrics fail (e.g., analysis of worst-case judgments in Section 6.4) and shows the complementary effect of combining object grounding, caption similarity, and feature correlation.
weaknesses: Limited dataset diversity in the meta-evaluation: The human judgment data was collected exclusively on reconstructions generated by a single model (MindEye2). Because different architectures produce distinct artifacts and failure distributions, evaluating metric alignment on only one model risks overfitting the evaluation metric to MindEye2-specific characteristics.

Incremental metric formulation: The SEED metric is essentially an unweighted average of three off-the-shelf tools (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT + Sentence Transformer, and EfficientNet). While practically effective, the algorithmic contribution of the metric itself is relatively straightforward.

Object F1 category constraint: Object F1 is constrained to 82 predefined COCO-based categories. While these cover common objects, they struggle with complex concepts, compositional relationships, or out-of-vocabulary salient elements, which can lead to zero-scores for semantically related scenes (as illustrated in Figure 11a).

Divided focus and marginal gains from Pairwise Hinge Loss: The introduction of the pairwise hinge loss ($L_{pair}$) feels somewhat decoupled from the primary focus on evaluation. Furthermore, the empirical gains on the strongest baseline (MindEye2) are very marginal (SEED improving from 0.474 to 0.475; Inception from 94.5% to 94.6%).

Computational complexity of the loss: The proposed triplet-based formulation in Eq. (8) exhibits $O(N^3)$ complexity over the batch size $N$, which can become computationally prohibitive for larger training batch sizes without specialized sampling.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: existing evaluation protocols in visual brain decoding (notably two-way identification metrics) are nearing saturation (>95%) while failing to penalize critical semantic errors (e.g., misidentifying objects or hallucinating wrong categories).

Comprehensive and rigorous human evaluation dataset: collecting ratings across 1,000 image pairs from 22 evaluators with high inter-rater reliability (ICC = 0.84) provides a solid benchmark for meta-evaluating visual brain decoding metrics.

The proposed composite metric (SEED) demonstrates statistically significant improvements in correlation with human judgment (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson) compared to all established baselines across multiple datasets (NSD and GOD).

Insightful diagnostic value and failure mode analysis: the breakdown into Object F1 and Cap-Sim provides interpretable insights into model weaknesses, such as quantifying 'semantic near-misses' (17-20%) and missing contextual details (8-10%) across state-of-the-art models.
Extensive robustness and ablation studies exploring alternative off-the-shelf model combinations (e.g., YOLO-World, BLIP-2, Qwen3-Embedding) and auxiliary cues (size, location, VLM-based classes).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an ensemble of existing pre-trained off-the-shelf tools (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT + Sentence Transformer, and EffNet) with an unweighted average, which represents somewhat incremental algorithmic novelty.

Reliance on a predefined list of 82 COCO-derived categories for Object F1 limits the open-vocabulary semantic breadth, potentially overlooking salient concepts outside this taxonomy unless explicitly adapted.

Susceptibility to out-of-distribution artifacts: as noted in the paper's own failure analysis, brain decoding outputs often contain unnatural visual distortions that cause image grounding and captioning models to fail or hallucinate, which directly impairs SEED's assessment.

The scope of evaluation is strictly restricted to semantic similarity; while justified by the authors, visual brain decoding also intrinsically values low-level/perceptual layout fidelity, and SEED does not integrate perceptual alignment into its unified score.

strengths: Addresses a critical and timely problem in visual brain decoding: existing evaluation metrics (notably 2-way identification accuracies) have largely saturated (often >95%) and fail to reliably capture semantic errors and human perceptual alignment.

Rigorously validated with a large-scale human evaluation dataset (1,000 pairs evaluated by 22 annotators on NSD, plus 50 pairs on GOD with 10 annotators) demonstrating high inter-rater agreement (ICC = 0.84 and 0.93) and statistically significant correlation improvements over prior metrics.

The multi-stage design of SEED (combining object grounding via threshold-averaged Object F1, caption similarity via Cap-Sim, and structural/scene representation via EffNet) is well-motivated and thoroughly ablated against various model backbones and alternative combinations.

Provides valuable diagnostic utility by uncovering concrete failure modes in state-of-the-art brain decoders (such as semantic near-misses and object-level reconstructions missing contextual details), offering actionable insights for future decoding research.
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the metric formulation is somewhat incremental, as SEED is an unweighted average of existing or adapted components (Grounding-DINO detection, GIT/Sentence-Transformer caption similarity, and EffNet embeddings).

Object F1 primarily relies on a predefined list of 82 categories (derived from COCO), which may limit the metric's sensitivity to fine-grained objects or out-of-vocabulary entities present in complex natural stimuli.

Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf captioning and detection foundation models can make the metric vulnerable to hallucinations or domain shifts caused by blurry and distorted reconstructions characteristic of visual decoding.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely issue: Existing visual brain decoding evaluation heavily relies on saturated two-way identification tasks (e.g., AlexNet, Inception, CLIP accuracy >95%) and rigid low-level metrics (SSIM, PixCorr) that fail to penalize severe semantic misalignments.

Rigorous human evaluation benchmark: The authors collected semantic and perceptual ratings from 22 annotators across 1,000 image pairs on the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and validated high inter-annotator reliability (ICC = 0.84), providing a solid ground truth for meta-evaluation.

Insightful failure mode analysis: The paper goes beyond benchmarking by identifying and quantifying systematic failure patterns in modern brain decoding models, such as semantic near-misses (e.g., dog substituted with cat) and loss of background/pose context despite correct object detection.

Comprehensive robustness checks: The authors evaluate metric stability across multiple alternative off-the-shelf components (e.g., YOLO-World, BLIP-2, Qwen-Embedding) and across datasets (NSD and GOD).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: SEED is essentially an unweighted average of three off-the-shelf components (Grounding-DINO detection F1, GIT caption similarity via Sentence-BERT, and EffNet feature correlation). The formulation is straightforward and mostly an engineering aggregation of existing tools.

Missing comparisons with modern general-purpose semantic/perceptual similarity metrics: While the paper compares against traditional decoding metrics (SSIM, PixCorr, AlexNet, SwAV, EffNet), it does not benchmark against newer learned perceptual and semantic image similarity metrics from the vision literature (e.g., DreamSim, LPIPS, or CLIP directional score).

Susceptibility to foundation model hallucination and OOD artifacts: Because visual brain reconstructions frequently contain severe blur, visual incoherence, or hybrid textures, vision-language backbones like GIT and Grounding-DINO are prone to severe misclassifications and hallucinations (as acknowledged in Section D.2 and Figure 10).

Ad-hoc equal weighting: The decision to simply divide the sum by 3 is heuristic; while avoiding overfitting, the paper lacks systematic analysis or optimization regarding how these three distinct feature spaces scale and contribute to human correlation across different stimulus distributions.
